title: Condemned by Pilate, Crucified, and Buried
summary: At dawn the council hands Jesus to Pilate, and Judas, seized with remorse, throws back the silver and hangs himself. Pilate, pressed by the chief priests and the crowd, releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be flogged and crucified. Mocked by soldiers, passersby, leaders, and fellow victims, Jesus dies with the cry of Psalm 22 on his lips; the temple veil tears, the earth shakes, and a centurion confesses him as the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea buries him, and the leaders have the tomb sealed and guarded.
story: Chapter 26 ended with Jesus condemned by the council and Peter weeping. Now the story moves from the Jewish court to the Roman one, since only the governor could order an execution. The chapter is the center toward which all of Matthew has been heading since the angel told Joseph that Jesus would save his people from their sins (1:21). The mocking title King of the Jews recalls the magi who came asking for the one born king of the Jews (2:2), and the Gentile centurion's confession recalls those first Gentile worshipers. The sealed and guarded tomb at the end sets the stage for the resurrection in chapter 28, and removes in advance the suggestion that the body was simply taken.
historical:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36. His title was prefect, confirmed by a stone inscription found at Caesarea in 1961 that names him prefect of Judea and records his dedication of a building to the emperor Tiberius. Josephus and the Jewish writer Philo describe him as harsh and provocative toward Jewish sensibilities, though he could also back down under pressure from crowds. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around AD 116, records that Christus, from whom the Christians took their name, was executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius. Together with Josephus, this makes the crucifixion of Jesus under Pilate one of the best attested facts of ancient history, accepted by nearly all historians whatever their beliefs.

Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves, violent criminals, and rebels against its rule, deliberately public and humiliating. Victims were usually flogged first, then made to carry the crossbeam to the place of execution, where they were fixed to the cross by ropes or nails and could take hours or days to die. In 1968 the heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan, with an iron nail still through it, was found in a first-century tomb in Jerusalem, confirming that the crucified could be buried in family tombs. The written charge posted above Jesus, King of the Jews, shows that Rome executed him as a royal pretender, a threat to Caesar.
cultural:
Several details carry meaning a first reader would catch. Washing the hands to declare innocence of bloodshed echoes Deuteronomy 21:6-9, a Jewish rite, and the crowd's reply takes responsibility on themselves in a traditional formula. The soldiers' mockery parodies a royal investiture: a scarlet military cloak for a purple robe, thorns for a crown, a reed for a scepter, and the salute given to the emperor. Offering wine mixed with a bitter substance may have been meant as a drug to dull pain, though Matthew's wording echoes Psalm 69:21, and Jesus refuses it. Dividing the victim's clothes was the executioners' perk, and Matthew's readers would hear Psalm 22:18.

The temple veil was the great curtain separating the holy place from the most holy place, which only the high priest entered, once a year on the Day of Atonement. Burial before sunset was required by the law (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), especially before a Sabbath. A rock-cut tomb with a rolling stone was the kind of family tomb that only the wealthy could afford, which is why Joseph of Arimathea's gift was costly, and it matches Isaiah 53:9, where the servant is with a rich man in his death.
literary: The chapter is built as a series of trials and verdicts in which, ironically, nearly everyone testifies to Jesus' innocence or identity. Judas calls his own act betraying innocent blood; Pilate's wife calls Jesus an innocent man; Pilate asks what evil he has done; and at the cross the centurion confesses him as Son of God. The mockers speak truth without knowing it: he saved others and cannot save himself, because he will not. The crucifixion scene is saturated with Psalm 22 (the division of clothes, the shaking heads, the taunt about trusting God, and the cry of forsakenness) and with Psalm 69. Matthew alone includes the dream of Pilate's wife, the hand washing, the saints raised after the earthquake, and the guard at the tomb. His citation in verses 9 and 10 combines words mainly from Zechariah 11:12-13 with themes from Jeremiah (a potter, a purchased field) and credits the prophecy to Jeremiah, the major prophet, a way of combining texts found in other ancient Jewish writing.

outline.t: Judas's remorse and death; the potter's field
The crucifixion and the mockery at the cross
Darkness, the death of Jesus, and the signs that follow

doctrines.note: The innocent one dies while the guilty Barabbas goes free, a picture the church has long read as substitution. The torn veil shows that his death opens access to God that the temple's sacrifices only pointed to (Hebrews 10:19-20).

Jesus enters the depth of human suffering: injustice, mockery, physical agony, abandonment by friends, and the experience of forsakenness voiced in Psalm 22. The sufferer who prays that psalm is never outside God's sight, and Christians find in it permission to lament honestly.
Jesus is executed under the charge King of the Jews and mocked as King of Israel. Matthew wants readers to see that the title is true: this is how Israel's Messiah reigns, from a cross.

words.note: Stauros, cross, originally an upright stake. It became the instrument of Roman execution and, by the reversal of the gospel, the central sign of the Christian faith. Jesus had told his disciples to take up their cross (16:24); here a stranger, Simon of Cyrene, is forced to carry his.

Katapetasma, curtain or veil. In the Greek Old Testament the word is used for the curtains of the tabernacle, including the inner veil before the most holy place. Its tearing from top to bottom, from God's side, is read as the opening of the way into God's presence, and also as a sign of judgment on the temple.

Enkataleipo, to forsake or abandon. It is the verb in Jesus' cry, quoting Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic and Hebrew. The psalm begins in abandonment and ends in praise and the turning of the nations to God. Jesus' cry expresses real anguish, and many readers also hear in it the whole psalm's hope.

christ: This is the center of what Christ has done. The King of the Jews wears a crown of thorns; the Son of God, taunted to come down from the cross, stays there, and so saves others by not saving himself. He dies as the innocent one in place of the guilty, as the righteous sufferer of Psalm 22, and as the servant of Isaiah 53 who was numbered with transgressors and buried with the rich. The signs at his death, the torn veil, the earthquake, the opened tombs, announce that his death breaks down the barrier between God and people and begins the defeat of death itself. The church confesses in the creed that he suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried, anchoring its faith in this public, datable event.

hard.q: What does “His blood be on us and on our children” mean, and how should it be read today?
hard.a: This cry in verse 25 has been one of the most misused lines in the Bible. For centuries it was cited to brand the Jewish people as a whole as Christ-killers and to justify contempt and violence against them. That use is a grave misreading. The crowd in Pilate's courtyard was a particular group of people in Jerusalem on one morning, stirred up by particular leaders, and they cannot speak for all Jews then or since. Matthew's own Gospel is written by a Jew about a Jewish Messiah whose first followers were all Jews, and it holds Pilate, the soldiers, Judas, and the disciples responsible as well. Some interpreters note that Matthew's readers would have linked the saying to the destruction of Jerusalem a generation later, as a judgment on that city, not on a people forever. Many also hear a deep irony: the blood of Jesus, which the crowd calls down in guilt, is the blood of the covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28). The church has come to confess that all humanity, including every Christian, stands among those for whom and because of whom Christ died, and the Catholic Church explicitly rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt at the Second Vatican Council in 1965.

questions: Pilate washed his hands and still handed Jesus over. Where are you tempted to think that declaring yourself uninvolved is the same as being innocent?
The mockers said he saved others but could not save himself. Why is the truth hidden in that taunt at the heart of the Christian faith?
Jesus prayed Psalm 22 from the cross. How might the psalms of lament help you bring your own darkest moments to God?
